web_blocks.html: Evaluating the GraniteShares 2x Long NBIS Daily ETF (NASDAQ: NBIL) requires dissecting two distinct layers of risk that are frequently conflated by retail participants. The first layer is the derivative wrapper itself: a daily-reset, swap-backed single-stock exchange-traded fund launched on October 7, 2025 under the Investment Company Act of 1940 [1][2]. The second layer is the underlying operating enterprise it tracks, Nebius Group N.V. (NASDAQ: NBIS), an Amsterdam-headquartered artificial intelligence infrastructure provider forged out of the 2024 geopolitical carve-out of Yandex N.V. [3][4]. Unlike a traditional equity where an investor owns a fractional claim on perpetual cash flows, an NBIL holder owns a daily-reset contract. Its exposure to Nebius Group resets to 200% at the close of every trading day [2][5].

To understand why NBIL exhibits extreme path dependency, evidenced by a 1-year total return of -61.48% as of November 2026 [1], one must trace the tumultuous corporate evolution of Nebius Group N.V. [3]. The underlying company began life as the international engineering and cloud-infrastructure arm of Yandex N.V., the Dutch-incorporated parent of Russia's dominant search and technology conglomerate founded by Arkady Volozh [3][6]. Following the February 2022 invasion of Ukraine, NASDAQ suspended trading in Yandex N.V. Class A shares, and Western sanctions froze the company's cross-border capital access [6][7]. Volozh stepped down from operational leadership, publicly condemned the war in 2023, and he later saw European Union sanctions against him lifted [6][8].

Between 2022 and mid-2024, Yandex N.V.'s board executed one of the largest geopolitical corporate divorces in modern technology history [3][4]. In July 2024, the Dutch parent finalized a $5.4 billion cash-and-stock divestiture of all Russian-based operations to a consortium of local buyers. It retained a select portfolio of international assets. A flagship GPU data center in Mäntsälä, Finland, an engineering talent base relocated across Europe and Israel, the Toloka AI data platform, the Avride autonomous driving unit, the TripleTen edtech business. A substantial minority equity stake in ClickHouse [3][4][9]. Rebranded as Nebius Group N.V. with Volozh returning as CEO, the company resumed trading on the NASDAQ Global Select Market under ticker NBIS on October 21, 2024 [3][10].

Once relisted, Nebius Group pivoted aggressively from a post-restructuring holding company into a pure-play "neocloud". Building and leasing massive clusters of NVIDIA graphics processing units (GPUs) for frontier AI training and inference [11][12]. In December 2024, the company raised $700 million in a private placement. NVIDIA, Accel, and Orbis Investments anchored that round [12]. Throughout 2025 and 2026, management scaled capital commitments at a blistering pace. In September 2025, it signed a five-year $17.4 billion to $19.4 billion GPU deal with Microsoft. In March 2026, it added a five-year Meta deal worth up to $27 billion ($12 billion dedicated plus a $15 billion backstop) [13][14].

web_blocks.takeaway: NBIL was launched in October 2025—directly into the teeth of Nebius Group's hyper-capex, convertible-debt, and hyperscaler-announcement volatility cycle—magnifying every execution delay and financing announcement by 2x daily.

web_blocks.html: GraniteShares launched NBIL on October 7, 2025, just weeks after Nebius announced its landmark Microsoft contract, to capture intense retail and tactical trader demand for amplified exposure to the AI neocloud theme [1][2][13]. By November 2026, NBIL had accumulated $130.88 million in assets under management (AUM) and averaged 6.49 million shares in daily trading volume. This comes with single-session spikes exceeding 32.95 million shares [1]. Under its Investment Company Act of 1940 structure, NBIL is not a passive buy-and-hold equity fund. It is a Regulated Investment Company (RIC) that distributes net investment income and realized capital gains annually. As a result, swap-generated short-term gains and Treasury collateral interest are taxed at ordinary income or short-term capital-gains rates rather than enjoying long-term equity deferral [2][5]. In addition, the structural mismatch between a hyper-volatile, capital-intensive infrastructure builder and a daily-reset 2x derivative wrapper has been brutal. Over its trailing one-year window, NBIL posted a -61.48% return. That loss shows how daily beta slippage erodes capital whenever an underlying stock swings widely [1][5].

To appreciate why NBIS itself generates such extreme daily volatility, one must also examine its dual-class governance and shareholder-base transition. Following the July 2024 divestiture, Nebius retained 69.02 million Class A shares in treasury alongside 219.47 million Class A shares and 33.55 million Class B shares outstanding as of December 31, 2025 [36]. Because Class B shares carry super-voting rights held primarily by founder Arkady Volozh and senior insiders, public Class A holders—and by extension NBIL swap holders—have limited governance recourse over management's capital-allocation decisions [6][36]. Between late 2024 and late 2026, the shareholder register rotated rapidly from post-sanctions special-situations funds into momentum-driven AI infrastructure traders, options market makers, and leveraged ETF arbitrage desks. That rotation pushed daily realized volatility far above traditional enterprise software peers.

web_blocks.mechanism: CONL seeks 200% of the daily percentage change of Coinbase Global (COIN) using total return swaps and daily rebalancing at the 4:00 PM ET close, while charging a ~1.15%–1.50% gross expense ratio plus implicit swap financing spreads [5].
web_blocks.outcome_numbers: During choppy 2023–2025 crypto-equity consolidation windows where annualized underlying volatility exceeded 80%–100%, daily-reset 2x single-stock ETFs suffered 15%–45% cumulative tracking drag relative to a naive 2x point-to-point expectation, turning flat or modestly positive underlying periods into deep net drawdowns [5].
web_blocks.lesson_for_symbol: NBIL shares the exact same mathematical engine as CONL. When an underlying stock like NBIS carries triple-digit implied volatility driven by multi-billion-dollar capex surprises, convertible bond issuances, and data-center commissioning delays, holding a 2x daily ETF across multi-month cycles converts volatility into permanent NAV decay.

web_blocks.title: Why Price-Blind Structural Analysis Separates Wrapper from Business
paragraphs: In this first pass, we deliberately strip away all market quotes and valuation multiples to ask two foundational questions: First, is the NBIL ETF wrapper engineered for long-term wealth compounding? Second, does the underlying Nebius Group operating business possess durable unit economics and self-funding cash conversion?

book_paragraphs: You and I need to start this analysis with a confession about architecture. Most investors look at a ticker like NBIL and treat it as a turbocharged proxy for an artificial intelligence cloud company. They hear about multi-billion-dollar contracts with Microsoft and Meta, they hear about clusters of cutting-edge NVIDIA chips humming inside Finnish data centers, and they assume that buying a two-times leveraged fund simply doubles their participation in that story.

That assumption is the fastest way to lose money in modern markets. When you buy NBIL—the GraniteShares 2x Long NBIS Daily ETF—you are not buying shares of Nebius Group N.V. You are not acquiring a claim on future data center cash flows, nor are you partnering with CEO Arkady Volozh for a five-year buildout. Instead, you are stepping into a two-story building constructed on shifting sand. On the ground floor sits Nebius Group, an extraordinarily ambitious, hyper-capital-intensive neocloud operator that was carved out of Yandex N.V. in 2024. On the upper floor sits a 1940 Act derivative wrapper that resets its leverage to exactly two hundred percent at four o'clock every single afternoon.

Let us walk through the ground floor first, because the origin story of Nebius Group is unlike anything else on the NASDAQ. Prior to 2022, Yandex N.V. was a Dutch holding company housing Russia's dominant internet search, ride-hailing, and cloud ecosystem. When war broke out in Ukraine in February 2022, NASDAQ froze the stock, Western sanctions descended, and the company spent more than two years negotiating a geopolitical separation. In July 2024, Yandex N.V. sold off all of its Russian businesses for 5.4 billion dollars in cash and stock. What remained inside the Dutch shell was a clean, Western-facing core: a flagship data center in Mäntsälä, Finland, hundreds of displaced systems engineers, a handful of emerging technology subsidiaries, and a fresh corporate identity—Nebius Group N.V.

When trading resumed on October 21, 2024, Volozh and his engineering team wasted no time. They saw a generational bottleneck in global computing: frontier AI labs and hyperscalers were starving for liquid-cooled data center megawatts and high-density NVIDIA GPU clusters. Nebius raised 700 million dollars in December 2024 from backers including NVIDIA and Accel, and then went on an infrastructure sprint that stunned Wall Street. By September 2025, Nebius signed a five-year agreement with Microsoft worth 17.4 billion to 19.4 billion dollars. By March 2026, it inked an even larger five-year framework with Meta worth up to 27 billion dollars.

book_subsections.title: The October 2025 Birth of a Tactical Wrapper
paragraphs: Right in the middle of that frenzy, on October 7, 2025, GraniteShares launched NBIL. The ETF was built for one narrow purpose: to deliver twice the single-day percentage return of NBIS, before fees and expenses. To achieve that, the fund does not simply buy shares on margin. It enters into total return swaps with institutional counterparties and holds cash and short-term Treasury equivalents as collateral. Because it is structured under the Investment Company Act of 1940 as a regulated investment company, any net income from those Treasury bills or realized gains from daily swap resets must be distributed to shareholders, often creating ordinary-income or short-term tax friction on top of fund expenses.

Here is the trap that catches uninitiated investors off guard. Because NBIL must deliver two times the daily return every single day, the fund manager has to buy more exposure after NBIS goes up and sell exposure after NBIS goes down. In a straight-line bull run, that mechanical buying can actually compound favorably. But in a volatile, two-way market—the exact environment created when a company announces twenty-seven billion dollars of annual capital expenditure alongside multi-billion-dollar convertible debt offerings—daily rebalancing acts like a ratchet in reverse. Over its first full year, NBIL posted a return of minus 61.48 percent, even as the underlying business grew revenue by triple digits.

There is one more structural detail from Nebius Group's origin that you and I cannot ignore: governance. When Yandex N.V. reorganized into Nebius Group, founder Arkady Volozh and insiders retained super-voting Class B shares—more than thirty-three and a half million of them alongside roughly two hundred nineteen million Class A shares. That dual-class structure gave Volozh the freedom to pivot aggressively from a cash-rich holding company into a forty-billion-dollar-plus CapEx sprint without needing permission from short-term public shareholders. For a common stockholder, that founder control can be a double-edged sword. For an NBIL holder, it means you are strapped into a two-times daily derivative on a founder-controlled capital-allocation engine that can announce a five-billion-dollar convertible bond or a ten-billion-dollar data center commitment overnight.

book_subsections.title: What History Teaches Us About Single-Stock 2x ETFs
paragraphs: If you want a real-world mirror for NBIL, look at GraniteShares' 2x Long COIN Daily ETF, known as CONL. Just like NBIL, CONL uses total return swaps and a four o'clock daily reset to double the daily moves of a hyper-volatile underlying business, Coinbase. Whenever crypto markets entered a choppy sideways consolidation with eighty to one hundred percent annualized volatility, CONL suffered fifteen to forty-five percent cumulative tracking drag compared to a simple two-times point-to-point return.

That is the base rate you and I are up against with NBIL. When an underlying stock swings violently on quarterly earnings surprises, debt raises, and power-grid bottlenecks, daily compounding stops being a tailwind and turns into a relentless tax on principal. That is why every serious institutional desk treats a single-stock two-times ETF strictly as an intraday or multi-day trading vehicle—and never as a long-term proxy for owning the business.

Think about the psychological trap this creates for retail investors. You read a compelling headline about Nebius signing a twenty-seven-billion-dollar framework with Meta or expanding into four gigawatts of contracted power, and you tell yourself that holding NBIL for six to twelve months is a smart way to double your upside. Yet every time the stock surges ten percent on a contract announcement and pulls back nine percent the following week on a convertible bond filing, the daily reset locks in the asymmetry against you. Over twelve months, those whipsaws add up to a minus 61.48 percent return—even when the underlying company's revenue is growing nearly sixfold. Before you ever touch a leveraged single-stock ETF, you must respect that the calendar itself is working against you whenever volatility is elevated.

Just as importantly, remember how young NBIL actually is. Launched on October 7, 2025, it has never lived through a full semiconductor downturn, a prolonged credit freeze, or a hyperscaler capital-expenditure digestion cycle. Its entire first year of existence unfolded during one of the strongest AI infrastructure buildouts in modern history, yet daily compounding friction still carved away more than sixty percent of its value. That single fact should anchor every expectation you carry into the rest of this dossier.
